title: New Slogan

jokes.text: Ben dramatically introduces the new city website with a fanfare ('Dun-da-da-dah!') — and the entire room ignores the features to fixate on a panda game on the front page.
jokes.setup: Ben excitedly presents the new website, listing useful civic features (parking tickets, business licenses, utility tax refunds) with obvious pride.
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately ignores all the useful features and becomes obsessed with Peebo the panda mascot that the designer casually dropped on the front page.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed cold open joke. Ben's earnest civic pride is immediately deflated by human nature — everyone gravitates to the shiny toy. It works because it's both character-specific (Ben the responsible, overlooked government worker) and universally relatable (we'd all click the panda). The escalation of features Ben lists before the panda reveal gives the punchline good room to breathe.

jokes.text: Wait, the panda's name is Peebo. Peebo.
jokes.setup: The room has already been distracted by the panda. Someone notices the panda has a name.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Peebo' is announced with reverent gravity, then repeated, as if this information is deeply significant.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'Peebo' is the joke — the pure absurdity of the name and the reverent way it's delivered. Economy is the strength here; two words do a lot of work. 'Peebo' is also just an inherently funny word.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Wait, you named the panda Gergich?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Well, I thought it would be funny!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Now everyone keeps calling it Gergich. They're way too invested in this panda's name.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Gergich! Here, Gergich! Such a cute little Gergich!

jokes.text: Look, you can even play ping-pong. [chaos erupts, people fight to play first]
jokes.setup: Ben mentions as an aside that the panda can play ping-pong.
jokes.punchline: The room immediately devolves into 'Me first! Me first!' fighting over a panda ping-pong game on a government website.
jokes.explanation: Escalation of the Peebo bit — the distraction grows from passive observation to active fighting. The childlike regression of government employees is the consistent joke, and this adds a nice second beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Did you guys see this? There's a ping-pong game on the website.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh my god, a ping-pong game?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm gonna destroy everyone at this.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're on.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Stand aside. I've been practicing my hand-eye coordination since 1987.

jokes.text: Congratulations, Ben. This is truly a fine panda game you made. Well done.
jokes.setup: Ben has worked hard on a civic website with real functionality. The room is obsessed with the panda game.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, Ben's partner, sincerely congratulates him — but for the panda game, completely undercutting his actual work in the most polite way possible.
jokes.explanation: This lands because it's Leslie — the most supportive person in the world — accidentally being the funniest person in the room by genuinely congratulating Ben for the wrong thing. Her complete sincerity makes it better than a sarcastic delivery would. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ben, this website is amazing! The tax calculator, the permit system, the public records database...

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Thanks, Leslie. I spent months on those features.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But you know what really makes this special? The Pawnee Bingo game in the corner!

jokes.text: I think if you click on the bamboo, it puts on a top hat.
jokes.setup: After being congratulated for 'the panda game,' Ben has accepted his fate.
jokes.punchline: He volunteers this additional panda feature — the top hat — with the flat delivery of a man who has given up defending his real work.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the cold open. Ben's deadpan acceptance — almost enthusiastically sharing the top hat detail — is a beautiful character moment. It suggests he actually spent more time on the panda than he'd admit. The specificity of 'the bamboo' adds to the absurdity. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: You look like Meryl Streep in Doubt.

jokes.text: I love you, Ben!
jokes.setup: Ben reveals the bamboo-to-top-hat feature.
jokes.punchline: Someone shouts 'I love you, Ben!' — a completely disproportionate emotional response to a panda wearing a hat.
jokes.explanation: A simple but effective button — the emotional hyperbole capping the cold open. Not sophisticated, but perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I wish I looked like Meryl Streep.

jokes.text: You look like Meryl Streep at the end of Ironweed.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what's wrong with Andy, who apparently looks terrible.
jokes.punchline: April compares him to a specific Meryl Streep film — and when Andy pushes back ('You wish'), the specificity of the Ironweed reference is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Punchy and specific — 'Ironweed' is an obscure enough film that the reference reads as genuinely withering rather than a generic insult. April's character (dry, detached, oddly cultured) makes the reference feel earned. Andy's 'You wish' response adds a layer of absurdity — he can't even tell if that's an insult.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: We've been driving around looking for bands all day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know, but we're going to find the perfect one for the festival!

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Our only accomplishment so far is multiple car crashes.

jokes.text: You wish. [to being compared to a disheveled, dying Meryl Streep]
jokes.setup: April insults Andy by comparing him to a tragic Meryl Streep character.
jokes.punchline: Andy responds 'You wish' as if this were a compliment — because from his perspective, being compared to anything Meryl Streep is a win.
jokes.explanation: Two words that tell you everything about Andy. He misunderstands the insult entirely and somehow turns it into a flex. The joke is fully character-specific — only Andy Dwyer would be flattered by this particular comparison. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Oh wow, you have insurance? Must be nice to show off like that.

jokes.text: Four car accidents. All these strangers' insurance information.
jokes.setup: Andy explains he's been driving all over Indiana scouting for bands and has 'nothing to show for it.'
jokes.punchline: What he DOES have to show is four car accidents and a collection of strangers' insurance cards — which he seems to regard as incidental rather than catastrophic.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Andy — the casual mention of four accidents as a minor footnote, and the specific detail of having collected 'all these strangers' insurance information' as if it's a hobby rather than a disaster. The economy is excellent; the disaster is implied, not explained.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I can't help you with that. I have a personal grudge from an unrelated dog park incident.

jokes.text: Ooh, I get it, you have car insurance. Why don't you brag about it?
jokes.setup: Andy has just mentioned having collected strangers' insurance info after four accidents.
jokes.punchline: April interprets this as Andy bragging about having car insurance — a wildly uncharitable and funny misread that also works as genuine April sarcasm.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for April — cutting, specific, and delivered as if Andy is somehow being pretentious. The twist is that she reframes his accident story as bragging, which is both absurd and totally within her worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have a very strict diet. I only eat red meat and eggs. Once, I ate a chili dog in the bathroom of a hospital while it was on fire.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It was a good day.

jokes.text: I'm boycotting until the owner apologizes for what she said to me at the dog park.
jokes.setup: Andy asks an Eagleton woman for live music venue recommendations.
jokes.punchline: She recommends a place — then immediately disqualifies it because she's boycotting due to a personal grievance from a dog park incident, delivered with complete self-seriousness.
jokes.explanation: A quick character sketch of Eagleton pretension — the kind of person who stages a principled boycott of a music venue over a dog park slight. Efficient background joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm allergic to turkey neck.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Turkey neck? I love turkey neck! It's my favorite part!

jokes.text: I hear Cozy's Bar is pretty packed on Thursdays. But I've never been because it's mostly middle-aged women and I'm allergic to turkey neck.
jokes.setup: The woman offers another venue recommendation.
jokes.punchline: She's never been because she's 'allergic to turkey neck' — a hilariously specific and mean description of older women's necks, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Unexpected specificity makes this land — 'allergic to turkey neck' as a reason to avoid a bar is genuinely original. The character is oblivious to her own cruelty, which is the satirical point about Eagleton types. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is like that moment in the Michael Jackson 'Thriller' video when he turns into a zombie and realizes he's a monster. Except instead of a monster, I'm becoming a government official. Which is basically the same thing.

jokes.text: Really? That's the best part. We should split a turkey sometime.
jokes.setup: The Eagleton woman says she's 'allergic to turkey neck' as a reason to avoid middle-aged women.
jokes.punchline: Andy completely misses the metaphor and responds as if she's talking about literal turkey, offering to share a turkey with her.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Andy — he hears 'turkey neck,' doesn't process the metaphor at all, and pivots to a sincere food invitation. 'We should split a turkey sometime' is a line only Andy Dwyer could say in this moment. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, this is a totally normal thing that people want. I'm sure plant nurseries get requests like this all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They don't.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well they should.

jokes.text: The chance for me to return your binder full of questions about the job. I think I answered all of them.
jokes.setup: Leslie meets with Grant Larson about a dream job opportunity and has obviously been intensely preparing.
jokes.punchline: Grant returns a physical binder full of Leslie's questions — implying a comical volume of advance preparation — and confirms he answered all of them.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie joke — her over-preparation manifesting as a physical binder of questions. Very character-specific, though the 'Leslie makes binders' joke is well-worn by season 6.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I hate paperwork. It's the worst part of my job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But yesterday I spent six hours color-coding my filing system by department, then alphabetized within each section, then created a cross-reference index with laminated tabs and a personalized legend.

jokes.text: Martha? I'm gonna need two hours worth of waffles.
jokes.setup: Leslie is meeting Grant for what should be a quick catch-up.
jokes.punchline: She orders 'two hours worth of waffles' — treating waffle quantity as a time measurement and revealing she intends to monopolize this man for two hours minimum.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Two hours worth of waffles' is gloriously Leslie — it merges her waffle obsession with her inability to be brief. Using time as a waffle unit of measurement is original and perfectly economic. Could only be Leslie Knope. Strong candidate for most quotable line in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm like the next Wolfgang Puck, except I can't cook.

jokes.text: This is like the parks equivalent of Bruce Springsteen pulling Courtney Cox onstage. I mean, one minute you're just a regular girl in the crowd, and the next minute you're dancing 10 feet away from freakin' Max Weinberg!
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing how exciting the national parks job offer is.
jokes.punchline: Her analogy goes from 'Bruce Springsteen pulls you onstage' (already a stretch) to the real excitement being '10 feet away from Max Weinberg' — completely burying the Springsteen lead in favor of the drummer.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is excellent — you expect the excitement to be Springsteen, but the punchline buries him for Max Weinberg, the E Street Band drummer. This is a real reference (Courtney Cox was pulled onstage in the 'Dancing in the Dark' video) deployed with a perfect comedic twist. Slightly long, which holds back economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Larry, I got you something special. This is a personalized gift, just for you.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, that's very thoughtful, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a ergonomic back support that's slightly too small, a stress ball filled with thumbtacks, and a framed photo of me photoshopped to look like I'm standing right behind you at all times.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because it's Larry. I mean, Jerry. Whatever.

jokes.text: Good! I hate paperwork. I hardly ever do it in my bed on a Saturday night while listening to old Spice Girls CDs.
jokes.setup: Grant tells Leslie the job is 'big picture' — no more boring paperwork.
jokes.punchline: Leslie enthusiastically agrees she hates paperwork, then immediately reveals via triple negative that she absolutely does paperwork in bed on Saturday nights to Spice Girls.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic self-betrayal — Leslie's protest is so detailed and specific ('on a Saturday night while listening to old Spice Girls CDs') that it's obviously autobiographical. The triple-negative structure ('I hardly ever do it') doing the heavy lifting of self-exposure. Extremely character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What is this?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's a voodoo doll. Of me. I made it myself.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why would you make a voodoo doll of yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't know, I thought it might be fun.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to poke it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: *pokes the doll*

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: *immediately falls down*

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: The voodoo! The voodoo is real!

jokes.text: I'm kind of like a skinny, handsome, Indian Mario Batali... who doesn't know how to cook.
jokes.setup: Tom is describing his vision for Tom's Bistro — his grand restaurateur persona.
jokes.punchline: After stacking flattering comparisons (skinny, handsome, Indian Mario Batali), he deflates it entirely: 'who doesn't know how to cook.'
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Tom Haverford joke. The setup builds with escalating self-flattery, then the final clause torpedoes the entire premise with cheerful self-awareness. The structure is textbook: pile on the credentials, then destroy them. 'Who doesn't know how to cook' is the ideal punchline for someone opening a restaurant. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We can just sit back and take it easy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Sit back? Take it easy? Ben, those are the two things I'm worst at. The opposite of that would be stand up and take it hard.

jokes.text: A Larry voodoo doll? Tom, that's so sweet. Thanks. [immediately pokes it, Larry says 'Ow!']
jokes.setup: Tom gives a gift to Ben and another colleague — a Larry voodoo doll.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately pokes the doll and Larry shouts 'Ow!' from off-screen, as if it actually works.
jokes.explanation: Solidly constructed Larry-abuse gag. The 'it actually works' twist is predictable but executed well with the timing. The 'I didn't even do anything' / 'The voodoo doll is reading my thoughts' extension is the better part.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: New York's slogan is 'I Love New York.' You know what Pawnee's slogan should be?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: 'Pawnee: First in Friendship, Fourth in Obesity.'

jokes.text: I didn't even do anything. The voodoo doll is reading my thoughts.
jokes.setup: Someone pokes the Larry voodoo doll and Larry shouts in pain. Then he clarifies no one touched the doll.
jokes.punchline: Larry theorizes the voodoo doll is 'reading his thoughts' — implying he was mentally torturing his own voodoo doll, and somehow this is his life.
jokes.explanation: The stronger half of the voodoo doll gag. The escalation from 'voodoo doll works' to 'voodoo doll reads my thoughts' is a great absurdist escalation, and it implies Larry's self-loathing is so complete that his psychic energy is hurting himself. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: They were serving whale meat. Illegally.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, that's horrible!

jokes.text: There is New York, the city that never sleeps. And then there is Glenwater, Florida, home of America's most violent Walmart parking lot.
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining how slogans can make a big difference to a city's identity.
jokes.punchline: He illustrates with two examples: NYC's famous slogan, then immediately undercuts it with 'Glenwater, Florida, home of America's most violent Walmart parking lot.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup/punchline with perfect structural contrast. The NYC slogan sets an expectation of grandeur; the 'Glenwater, Florida' punchline is a great comedic inversion. 'Most violent Walmart parking lot' is specific enough to be genuinely funny and taps into real cultural anxiety about Walmart parking lots.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I don't know why you're here, but welcome to Pawnee Parks and Recreation. I'm Leslie Knope, Deputy Director. I have no idea what that camera is doing here, but I'm going to assume it's for something important and prestigious.

jokes.text: No. No, we're not gonna do that. We're gonna sit forward and take it hard.
jokes.setup: Ben says they can 'sit back and take it easy' now that the website does the work.
jokes.punchline: Leslie rejects the entire premise, declaring they will 'sit forward and take it hard' — a maximally Leslie response that accidentally sounds unintentionally suggestive.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Ben's baffled 'Um, what?' reaction and the unintended double entendre of 'sit forward and take it hard.' Leslie is completely oblivious, making it better. Strong character integration — Leslie's work ethic articulated in the most accidentally inappropriate way possible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, come talk to the camera with me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we've talked about this. You can't keep using these talking head segments to live out your fantasy of being romantically involved with the cameraman.

jokes.text: So this was one of Eagleton's top sushi restaurants. But you can't out-run the whale meat police forever.
jokes.setup: April is showing Tom restaurant spaces, starting with a former Eagleton sushi restaurant.
jokes.punchline: It closed because 'you can't outrun the whale meat police forever' — implying the restaurant was serving whale meat, delivered with April's signature casual-dark affect.
jokes.explanation: Unexpected and dark — the idea of a whale meat police unit existing and eventually catching up with an Eagleton sushi restaurant is absurdly specific. 'You can't outrun the whale meat police forever' works as both a statement about Eagleton excess and a standalone absurdist line. Extremely quotable. Only April would deliver this as a neutral fact.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used to represent a company or organization. It's catchy, it's easy to remember, and it encapsulates the essence of what that brand is all about.

jokes.text: That's where the politicians will sit, this is where the connected guys will bring their goomahs.
jokes.setup: Tom is touring a potential restaurant space with grandiose dreams.
jokes.punchline: He's already mentally allocated the restaurant to mob-adjacent VIPs and their 'goomahs' (mistresses) — Sopranos-tier ambitions for a man whose restaurant doesn't exist yet.
jokes.explanation: Tom's delusions of grandeur are on full display — 'goomahs' is a Sopranos-adjacent word that perfectly captures his fantasy of running a prestige Italian joint. Character-specific, quickly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Well, what we're seeing here is enthusiasm at a moderate level, which is to say, not particularly enthusiastic. The crowd's response could be described as lukewarm, or if I'm being generous, room temperature.

jokes.text: This press junket is a brilliant idea, isn't it? Mr. Strange Cameraman Who I Never Met.
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing a confessional talking head in the mockumentary format.
jokes.punchline: She addresses the camera operator with an elaborate pretense that they are strangers — 'Mr. Strange Cameraman Who I Never Met' — as if performing ignorance for the documentary format.
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about the mockumentary format — Leslie is transparently gaming the documentary by pretending to be a stranger to the cameraman so it looks more 'legit.' The follow-up Ben refusal makes it better. Smartly constructed self-referential moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I want to rebrand myself. I'm going to change my name to something more sophisticated. How about... Juana?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Juana just means 'Joan' in Spanish.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Fine, then I'll be... Juanita.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: That means 'little Joan.'

jokes.text: And a slogan is a series of words that have a meaning.
jokes.setup: Perd Hapley the reporter is asking Leslie about the slogan poll.
jokes.punchline: He defines a slogan as 'a series of words that have a meaning' — a definition so uselessly obvious it suggests he has no idea what a slogan is.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Perd Hapley joke — his defining characteristic is that he states obvious things with maximum gravitas. 'A slogan is a series of words that have a meaning' captures him perfectly: technically correct, completely useless, delivered with anchor confidence. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: That's a really thoughtful question. Let me think about that for a second.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Can you suck my dick?

jokes.text: Well, the story of my interest level is: It's medium.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Perd her favorite slogan would be 'Storied past, bright future.'
jokes.punchline: Perd responds by framing his reaction as a 'story' (his verbal tic of over-narrating) — 'the story of my interest level is: it's medium.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. Perd's defining tic — framing everything as a 'story' — is used here to deliver the most Perd-possible reaction: unnecessary narrative packaging around an underwhelming verdict. 'The story of my interest level is: it's medium' is perfectly constructed and extremely quotable. Maximum character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I am Duke Silver. And I play the saxophone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The saxophone is like a woman. You have to be gentle with her, but firm. And sometimes you have to blow into her really hard until she screams.

jokes.text: Isn't 'Juan' a man's name? / No, it means 'flower.' / I think it means 'John.'
jokes.setup: Joan wants to rebrand as 'Juan Callamezzo.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie asks if Juan is a man's name; Joan insists it means 'flower'; Ben correctly notes it means 'John.' Joan is completely wrong and totally confident.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure works well — escalating corrections with Joan doubling down confidently on wrong information. Ben's flat correction ('I think it means John') is the perfect deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: According to this online poll, the top choice for the new park name is 'Butt Lake Park.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Apparently some juvenile radio hosts got their listeners to vote for it as a prank.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They hijacked our entire civic process!

jokes.text: Wow, that's a very thoughtful question, Crazy Ira. [beat] Yes, yes, I do.
jokes.setup: Crazy Ira from the 'Crazy Ira and the Douche' radio show asks Leslie a genuinely serious question about civic integration.
jokes.punchline: Leslie is visibly shocked that Crazy Ira asked something thoughtful, pauses, then answers earnestly — the beat before her 'Yes' doing all the comedic work.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the pregnant pause — Leslie cannot believe Crazy Ira asked something intelligent. The beat before 'Yes, yes, I do' contains the whole joke. Effective use of the mockumentary's ability to let silence do the work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so frustrated with democracy right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. I'm just going to become a benevolent dictator. Here's what I'm going to do: mandatory voting, three-day weekends, all desserts are now vegetables, and I'm going to make it illegal to not have fun on Friday nights.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... actually not terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right? I'm getting a sash made.

jokes.text: Follow-up question, Leslie — show us your boobs!
jokes.setup: Crazy Ira asked a shockingly thoughtful civic question. Leslie compliments it and answers seriously.
jokes.punchline: The follow-up is 'show us your boobs' — the thoughtful question was a setup to make the inevitable vulgarity land harder through contrast.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely structural — the thoughtful question was bait, and this is the trap. The contrast makes the vulgarity funnier than it would be in isolation. Cheap in isolation, but the misdirection structure elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As supreme leader, I'm making it illegal to use the word 'maybe.' From now on, it's 'yes' or 'no.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of hot.

jokes.text: Will this fit on a bumper sticker? [reporter asks about the slogan]
jokes.setup: Leslie is fielding press questions about the new town slogan in a press junket montage.
jokes.punchline: After 'show us your boobs,' the next reporter's question is mundane but hilariously practical: 'Will this fit on a bumper sticker?'
jokes.explanation: Quick comedic punctuation in the press junket montage — the normality of the question is funny after the chaos of the Douche's segment. Functional filler joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm wearing my hat backwards. It's a rebellious statement about conformity and societal expectations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The bill usually faces forward, right? But I've inverted it. That takes courage.

jokes.text: Honey, he is sex on a stick.
jokes.setup: Andy has arrived at a jazz club to scout bands. He notices the crowd's enthusiasm for the performer.
jokes.punchline: A fan describes the performer as 'sex on a stick' — completely unexpected given what we're about to learn about who the performer is.
jokes.explanation: Works as setup for the Duke Silver reveal — the 'sex on a stick' reaction lands harder once you know who's performing. On first watch, it's just funny; on rewatch, it's part of the joke that Ron Swanson is genuinely this alluring to women when he's Duke Silver.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So I was like, yo, that's totally dope and fly, homie. We should hang and do the thing where we... um... Netflix and chill? Is that still a thing? Because I'm very cool and current with the youths.

jokes.text: A smooth and silky evening to you all. On nights like this, when the cold winds blow, and the air is awash in the swirling eddies of our dreams, come with me and find safe haven... in a warm bathtub full of my jazz.
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson, who is gruff and no-nonsense, secretly performs jazz under the persona 'Duke Silver.' Andy watches from the crowd.
jokes.punchline: Duke Silver's patter is the complete opposite of Ron — florid, romantic, deeply purple prose — culminating in 'a warm bathtub full of my jazz.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a series highlight. 'A warm bathtub full of my jazz' is an objectively great line — romantic in intent, absurdly physical in metaphor. The comedy is entirely in the contrast between Duke Silver's velvet romanticism and Ron Swanson's usual stoic, three-word sentences. The escalating purple prose ('swirling eddies of our dreams') is perfect. High quotability, high rewatch value, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not going to rate Emma Watson's appearance. She's an incredibly talented actress and UN Women Goodwill Ambassador who has accomplished more by age 25 than most people do in a lifetime. Let's focus on her professional achievements and her advocacy work for gender equality.

jokes.text: Andy sees Ron Swanson perform as Duke Silver and has a visible reaction of disbelief/recognition [Uh!]
jokes.setup: Andy is scouting for bands and watches the jazz performer.
jokes.punchline: Andy recognizes Ron Swanson performing as 'Duke Silver' — his audible/visual reaction ('Uh!') is the entire beat.
jokes.explanation: Reaction beats are hard to score in transcript form, but Andy's shocked recognition of Ron-as-Duke-Silver is a big comedic moment that the audience shares with him. The impact is high because we've been set up by the 'sex on a stick' fan reaction — now we see who she was talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Listen Leslie, you gotta objectify women if you want to raise money for charity. That's just how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, Ira, that's not how it works. We can raise money without degrading women.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Well then I'm pulling my donation. Your moral stance just cost the children's hospital fifty bucks.

jokes.text: The current leader is 'Pawnee, welcome to Douche nation.'
jokes.setup: Leslie excitedly asks what slogan is leading the poll.
jokes.punchline: The leading slogan is 'Welcome to Douche nation' — thanks to Crazy Ira and the Douche flooding the poll.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the setup of the online poll — democracy immediately weaponized for juvenile purposes. Works as an escalating disaster joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not me. I've never been to a jazz concert in my life.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, I literally have your album.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't write it. Someone stole my identity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your name is on it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They're very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Besides, that album was made in the '70s. I was just a young man back then. Very confused. Could've easily become a jazz musician. Glad I didn't.

jokes.text: I'm not a dictator. If I were a dictator, I would throw the Douche in prison without a trial. I would be a very strong dictator, and you would be my bodyguard, and you would lead my army.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why they had a write-in option (democracy) and pivots to what she would do as a dictator.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's dictator fantasy is very specific and includes assigned roles for Ben — it's an entirely sincere, detailed vision she's clearly thought about.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie — the democracy-loving, institutions-respecting public servant — has clearly already planned out her dictatorship in some detail, including org chart assignments for Ben. The specificity makes it funny; the character contradiction makes it great.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, your woodworking is like a Craftsman tool commercial from 1987. Oddly specific, but I respect it.

jokes.text: Okay, I know we should figure out how to fix this. But I'm starting to get kind of turned on imagining you as a dictator, is that bad? / No, it's okay.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described her detailed dictator fantasy with Ben as bodyguard/army commander.
jokes.punchline: Ben admits he's getting turned on by the dictator fantasy; Leslie assures him this is fine — both responses are completely earnest.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic beat for a married couple — Ben's completely honest confession and Leslie's immediate, unbothered validation ('No, it's okay') is genuinely sweet and funny. The joke works on character grounds: these two have the most earnest relationship on television, and their matter-of-fact discussion of being turned on by authoritarianism is peak Ben-and-Leslie energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I keep Duke Silver secret because if everyone at the Parks Department found out, the office would be flooded with lingerie.

jokes.text: Backwards hat... shows a real lack of respect for authority. I like that.
jokes.setup: Leslie has arrived at the radio station wearing a backwards cap to appear 'chill' to the shock jocks.
jokes.punchline: Crazy Ira approves of her backwards hat for the wrong reason — seeing it as anti-authority — while Leslie's intent was the opposite (to seem cool/relatable).
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony of Leslie's backwards hat being read as transgressive (exactly wrong) is a nice quick gag. Her cringe attempt at being cool is a reliable Leslie comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Okay, here's a body part. Guess whose it is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Is that... a butt?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: It's my mother's butt.

jokes.text: I'm just psyched to be in the studio, you know? I'm just...chillin' in the studes with my dudes.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to appear laid-back to Crazy Ira and the Douche, claiming she's just there to hang.
jokes.punchline: 'Chillin' in the studes with my dudes' — a forced, terminally unhip attempt at slang that immediately reveals she's the opposite of chill.
jokes.explanation: 'Chillin' in the studes with my dudes' is a great cringe line — the rhyme 'studes/dudes' sounds like something a parent generates by guessing at youth slang. Highly quotable, deeply in character for Leslie's attempt to code-switch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that was exactly as dignified and empowering as it sounds.

jokes.text: First of all, I would rate her acting as an 'A.'
jokes.setup: Crazy Ira asks Leslie to rate Emma Watson's boobs on a scale from 1 to 'ga-ga-ga-going.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots to rating Emma Watson's acting — both dodging the question and revealing she can't even engage with the premise.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie moment — her inability to engage with the sexist premise reveals itself through her default to respectful advocacy. 'I would rate her acting as an A' is both a perfect dodge and an involuntary character confession. Only Leslie Knope would respond to this exactly this way. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not trying to be cool or anything, but hear me out. We need to invest in this park expansion, yo. It's going to be totally lit, fam. No cap, this is going to change our community, and that's the tea.

jokes.text: A minus. / More like double D minus.
jokes.setup: Leslie reluctantly gives Emma Watson's boobs an 'A minus' rating.
jokes.punchline: The host immediately corrects it to 'double D minus' — a bra cup size pun that reframes Leslie's grade as a bra size.
jokes.explanation: The pun is clean and fast — 'double D minus' works on both levels simultaneously. Not highbrow, but technically well-executed wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: We're Crazy Ira and the Douche, and we're here to help you find your lost item.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: That's right, Ira. What have you lost?

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Well, I've lost my dignity. Have you seen it?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: No, but I did see Leslie Knope. We're Crazy Ira and the Douche — we'll find your lost item, but we can't find Leslie a man!

jokes.text: Me so horny! I knew it. I knew it.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been coerced into participating in the 'rate celebrities' boobs' segment.
jokes.punchline: The host's 'Me so horny' declaration and smug 'I knew it' — as if he's proven Leslie secretly wanted this — is both juvenile and perfectly captures the bad-faith trap she's in.
jokes.explanation: Weakest of the radio station jokes — 'Me so horny' is a dated reference and the 'I knew it' is lazy. It works as character establishment for the Douche but isn't clever. Below-average craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to kill this version of myself. Destroy him completely. Wipe him out of existence.

jokes.text: I am Duke Silver. / I have a twin brother. [repeated back and forth as both explanations fail]
jokes.setup: Andy has confronted Ron about being Duke Silver. Ron doesn't want his cover blown.
jokes.punchline: Ron first denies it ('I have a twin brother'), then admits it, then tries to re-deny it — creating a comedic loop of denial and admission.
jokes.explanation: The 'twin brother' instinct-denial followed by immediate honest admission creates a great double-back structure. Ron trying to re-deploy the twin brother excuse after already confessing is the best beat — he knows it won't work but has nothing else. Very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Duke Silver, you were a good man. A saxophonist. A lover. And now you're gone. Rest in peace, you beautiful bastard.

jokes.text: The only other people who know are Tom and April. So, please, keep it to yourself. / Are you kidding me? You are really good! You are, like, the saxophone player for the California-raisins-good.
jokes.setup: Ron reveals only Tom and April know about Duke Silver and asks Andy to keep it secret.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately launches into enthusiastic praise — 'California-raisins-good' — completely ignoring the secrecy request, too excited to honor it.
jokes.explanation: 'California-raisins-good' is a perfectly Andy compliment — specific, retro, and enthusiastic in a way only Andy would be. The California Raisins reference is specific enough to be funny as a compliment scale. Andy's inability to honor the privacy request because he's too impressed is classic character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The slogan we chose was offensive to multiple groups.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I voted for it.

jokes.text: If my secret got out, this office would be waist-deep in women's undergarments.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining why he needs to keep Duke Silver a secret.
jokes.punchline: His stated reason: the office would be 'waist-deep in women's undergarments' — a completely deadpan, very Ron assessment of his own sex appeal.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Waist-deep in women's undergarments' is the most Ron Swanson possible reason — stated as practical logistics rather than as boasting, yet revealing complete confidence in his own irresistibility. The specific image of the office flooded to waist level with thrown underwear is both absurdist and perfectly delivered in his deadpan. Extremely quotable, maximum character integration.

jokes.text: You're gonna play right after Bobby knight ranger. It's a night ranger cover band where they only wear red sweaters.
jokes.setup: Andy is booking Ron/Duke Silver for the unity concert despite Ron's refusal.
jokes.punchline: He describes the opening act — 'Bobby Knight Ranger,' a Night Ranger cover band where 'they only wear red sweaters' — as if this context makes performing more appealing.
jokes.explanation: 'Bobby Knight Ranger' is a brilliant bit of absurdist specificity — a Night Ranger cover band named after Indiana basketball coach Bobby Knight, with the added detail that they 'only wear red sweaters' (a reference to Knight's red sweater and chair-throwing incident). This is a deep, layered Indiana-specific joke delivered with total Andy sincerity. The detail that they ONLY wear red sweaters is the perfect absurdist constraint. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Schindler's Lunch is going to be a Holocaust-themed restaurant. It's going to fail.

jokes.text: Hard to believe this is a fan game for your radio listeners.
jokes.setup: Leslie is being forced to play 'boobs or ass' as the final segment on the shock jock radio show.
jokes.punchline: She responds with withering sarcasm — 'Hard to believe this is a fan game for your radio listeners' — while still playing along.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's dry sarcasm breaking through her 'chill' act — a good character beat showing the effort it's taking to maintain her persona. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We need to move this dinosaur.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You can't move that dinosaur.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's load-bearing.

jokes.text: I never knew that objectifying women could be so much fun.
jokes.setup: Leslie has survived the entire 'boobs or ass' segment and is wrapping up with the hosts.
jokes.punchline: She deadpans 'I never knew that objectifying women could be so much fun' — 100% sarcasm, but the hosts take it as a genuine endorsement.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's tight-lipped sarcasm breaking through perfectly. The joke also works because the hosts are so oblivious they probably take it as sincere. Character-specific and cleanly delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Our website got hacked and they defaced our beloved panda mascot inappropriately.

jokes.text: Or you know what would also be kind of dope for the people of Douche nation to do? It's vote for another slogan. Like, you know, 'Storied past, bright future'? But... I don't care. I don't give a fart, bros.
jokes.setup: The hosts try to get more 'Douche nation' votes for the slogan poll. Leslie sneaks in a pitch for her preferred slogan while pretending to be indifferent.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't give a fart, bros' — Leslie's cringe attempt at profanity-adjacent slang while simultaneously trying to influence the vote she claims not to care about.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't give a fart, bros' is a great Leslie line — she can't even bring herself to swear, so 'fart' substitutes, and 'bros' is her trying to maintain the cool persona. But the whole paragraph is transparently trying to influence the vote she claims to be indifferent to. The contradiction between her words and intent is perfectly Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I miss doing actual work. You know, getting my hands dirty, dealing with potholes, talking to constituents about their sewage problems.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of sweet that you miss that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know! Most people hate that stuff, but I loved it. I loved the grunt work.

jokes.text: Hey, Crazy Ira, have you seen my stick? / Where's your stick? / I don't know. / Lesbo Baggins, you know where my stick is? / You... / Oh! Found my stick. / Where did you find it? / Up Leslie Knope's butt!
jokes.setup: Leslie has just attempted her subtle slogan-plug and is about to leave.
jokes.punchline: The Douche performs a bit about a 'stick' being 'up Leslie Knope's butt' — the 'Stick Up the Butt' slogan manifested as live performance art, with 'Lesbo Baggins' as a Leslie nickname.
jokes.explanation: The joke is more about Leslie's mortification than the bit itself — 'Lesbo Baggins' is creative as a portmanteau insult, but the rest is crude without much craft. Works as cringe comedy in context; the callback to the slogan is a nice structural touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Larry, we need you to help us move this equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. Happy to help.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'll just... I'll get my end over here...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Larry, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm stuck. I wedged myself between the desk and the filing cabinet somehow.

jokes.text: Jewish Greg, whatever we're paying you, it's not enough.
jokes.setup: Immediately after the 'stick up the butt' bit, someone named 'Jewish Greg' apparently played sound effects or otherwise contributed.
jokes.punchline: A sincere compliment to 'Jewish Greg' — the nickname itself and the over-the-top gratitude for apparently minimal work is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist background joke — 'Jewish Greg' as a radio-show nickname is very true to the world of shock jock radio (where everyone has a handle), and the sincere praise for him is a nice character detail. Minor but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I have a secret too. I... I don't always wash my hands after I go to the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not a secret, that's just poor hygiene.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm working on it!

jokes.text: Damn it, I almost pulled that off. / No, you really didn't.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just suffered total humiliation at the radio station.
jokes.punchline: Leslie genuinely believes she 'almost pulled that off' — Ben's flat 'No, you really didn't' is the loving but brutally honest correction.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-line exchange — Leslie's delusional optimism met with Ben's loving bluntness. 'No, you really didn't' is the ideal response: no elaboration needed, maximum truth. Strong economy and character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't understand milk percentages. Like, why is 2% milk only 2% milk? What's the other 98%?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Water.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. So why don't they just call it water with a little milk in it?

jokes.text: Good-bye, Duke Silver. May you rest... in jazz.
jokes.setup: Ron has decided to retire his Duke Silver persona to protect his secret and is ceremonially closing the saxophone case.
jokes.punchline: 'May you rest... in jazz' — a jazz riff on 'rest in peace,' delivered with Ron's funereal gravity toward an alter ego.
jokes.explanation: Episode highlight. 'May you rest in jazz' is near-perfect — the wordplay is clean (rest in peace → rest in jazz), the delivery context (Ron solemnly eulogizing his own alter ego) is inherently absurd, and the line only works because we know both Ron and Duke Silver. Maximum character integration, exceptional economy. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so one time I may have convinced my entire family to invest in a timeshare in Branson, Missouri. Not even a nice one. We all got really mad at each other for like two years.

jokes.text: Yeah, yeah. I voted for that one. [the 'home of the stick up Leslie Knope's butt' slogan]
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the hackers hijacked her poll with the 'stick up Leslie's butt' slogan — and is asking for help fixing it.
jokes.punchline: The IT guy casually reveals he personally voted for the joke slogan — he's one of them.
jokes.explanation: Good unexpected turn — the expert she's hiring for help voted for the problem. Clean structure and great economy ('Yeah, yeah. I voted for that one.' in response to her describing it as the joke slogan).

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Citizen
dialogue.line: Our city's new slogan should be 'Pawnee: Where the Chips Are Always Sideways and the Salsa Dreams of Motorcycles.'

jokes.text: Just PayPal me some bitcoins when you get a chance.
jokes.setup: The IT guy says he can fix Leslie's problem in two minutes.
jokes.punchline: He asks to be paid via 'PayPal me some bitcoins' — a deliberately confused mashup of payment methods that reveals he might not be as expert as claimed.
jokes.explanation: The PayPal/bitcoin conflation is funny as a character detail — either he's genuinely confused or he's being deliberately difficult. Leslie's 'What?' reaction (implied) completes the beat. Good economy.

jokes.text: I love it, because it reminds me of the cafeteria in a haunted nursing home, but that's just me.
jokes.setup: April is showing Tom a very rough restaurant space — a former donut/tire shop.
jokes.punchline: April enthusiastically loves the space precisely because it 'reminds me of the cafeteria in a haunted nursing home' — which she offers as if it's a selling point.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'The cafeteria in a haunted nursing home' is an incredibly specific, original image that could only come from April — and she offers it with genuine enthusiasm ('I love it, because...') and self-awareness ('but that's just me'). The casual '...but that's just me' understatement is perfect. Maximum April character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 1
dialogue.line: That should be 'we're,' not 'were.'

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 2
dialogue.line: Actually, it's 'our,' not 'are.'

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 3
dialogue.line: No, the whole thing should say 'Pawnee: First in Friendship, Fourth in Obesity.'

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 1
dialogue.line: That's not even a grammar issue!

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 2
dialogue.line: Well, 'obesity' should be capitalized if it's part of the slogan.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, let's just... let me fix this.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 3
dialogue.line: Wait, shouldn't there be a comma after 'Friendship'?

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 1
dialogue.line: No, a semicolon!

dialogue.speaker: Citizen 2
dialogue.line: An em dash!

jokes.text: This is the last listing I have that isn't an active crime scene.
jokes.setup: The realtor has been showing Tom terrible spaces that keep getting worse.
jokes.punchline: This is her last listing 'that isn't an active crime scene' — implying there are multiple listings that ARE active crime scenes in her portfolio.
jokes.explanation: A great throwaway line — 'not an active crime scene' as a property listing qualifier implies a specific and depressing real estate market. The line works because it's stated as a neutral fact. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so proud of myself for delegating this project. I gave clear instructions, set realistic deadlines, and trusted my team to execute.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Leslie. How did it turn out?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, they installed the sign backwards.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Backwards?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It now says 'Welcome to Pawnee' but it's facing the other direction, so everyone driving into town just sees the back of a sign.

jokes.text: We stretched ourselves too thin by expanding to a second location. / You opened another dinosaur-themed restaurant? / No, another Steven Spielberg-themed restaurant. The German place downtown... Schindler's Lunch.
jokes.setup: The Jurassic Fork owner explains why his restaurant failed — he expanded to a second location.
jokes.punchline: 'Schindler's Lunch' — a Holocaust-themed restaurant named after Schindler's List. The twist from 'dinosaur' to 'Spielberg' to 'Schindler' is a perfect three-step joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. The structure is impeccable: (1) setup establishes a Spielberg theme, (2) misdirect to dinosaurs, (3) the actual answer reveals the catastrophically wrong reading of 'Spielberg-themed' — a German restaurant called 'Schindler's Lunch.' The pun itself (Schindler's List → Lunch) is clean and fast, but the context (someone actually opened a Holocaust-themed lunch spot) is gloriously dark. High originality, perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What if I'm not actually good at my job? What if I've just been lucky?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're not lucky. You work hard. And you're very good at your job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How do you know?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because I've seen you work. And also, if you were just lucky, you would have won the lottery by now.

jokes.text: I think you may have misunderstood what people liked about Jurassic Fork.
jokes.setup: The Jurassic Fork owner has revealed he opened 'Schindler's Lunch.'
jokes.punchline: Tom's response is a masterclass in understatement — 'I think you may have misunderstood what people liked about Jurassic Fork' — rather than addressing the much more obvious problem.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Schindler's Lunch reveal. Tom's gentle, euphemistic correction avoids addressing the Holocaust angle entirely and instead focuses on the restaurant concept failure — which is both funnier and more Tom-appropriate than confronting the real issue. The understatement does enormous comedic work. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Wait, which way are we supposed to be facing?

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Does it matter? We're all just walking in circles anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I haven't been this confused since they changed the font on the government forms.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, everyone just... take a deep breath. We'll figure this out together as a team.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm pretty sure we came in from that direction. Or maybe that was the way out?

jokes.text: No can do. That's a load-bearing T-Rex.
jokes.setup: Tom is considering the Jurassic Fork space but suggests moving the T-Rex prop.
jokes.punchline: The owner refuses — 'That's a load-bearing T-Rex' — stated with complete architectural seriousness, as if this is a factual structural reality.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'Load-bearing T-Rex' is a perfect absurdist concept — the architectural term applied to a decorative dinosaur, stated with complete deadpan conviction. The 'load-bearing' descriptor is the key: it's the exact word you'd use for a real structural element, which makes the absurdity hit harder. Extremely quotable, excellent economy.

jokes.text: You didn't somehow get the email addresses for every person who voted for the 'Stick up the butt' slogan and then write each of them a personalized heartfelt email telling them to do the right thing and vote for a real slogan?
jokes.setup: Ben asks Leslie if she did something specific and very Leslie-like that she agreed not to do.
jokes.punchline: The question describes exactly what Leslie did in exhaustive detail — 'personalized heartfelt email' is the key — delivered as an incredulous negative.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Ben's question (he knows exactly what she did) is the comedy — the 'personalized heartfelt email' detail is perfect Leslie behavior. His disbelieving negative question format when he clearly already knows the answer is a great character moment for both of them.

jokes.text: Are you crazy? What a crazy talk you just did with your funny words.
jokes.setup: Ben has described exactly what Leslie did, in question form.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's denial is so flustered and obviously guilty that 'What a crazy talk you just did with your funny words' is not a denial at all — it's a confession.
jokes.explanation: 'What a crazy talk you just did with your funny words' is a great flustered-denial line — the sentence construction breaks down under Leslie's guilt, which makes it funnier than a smooth denial. The rhythm of the phrase ('crazy talk you just did with your funny words') is appealingly weird. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Look what they did to Peebo. He's wearing a hat made of penises.
jokes.setup: Hackers attacked the city website in retaliation for Leslie's emails.
jokes.punchline: The hackers' revenge: Peebo the panda is now wearing a hat made of penises — announced with Ben's devastated solemnity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the cold open. The comedy works on multiple levels: (1) Peebo is the one thing Ben cared about from the website, (2) the panda's hat callback (earlier he wore a top hat in game) is now a hat of penises, (3) Ben's delivery of 'He's wearing a hat made of penises' with apparent heartbreak is extremely funny. The structure connecting the cold open panda game to the hack payoff is genuinely well-written.

jokes.text: Have I really pulled my last bloated raccoon carcass from a public fountain?
jokes.setup: Leslie is reflecting on whether she should take the national parks job, which would mean moving away from nuts-and-bolts park work.
jokes.punchline: The specific task she's nostalgic for is 'pulling bloated raccoon carcasses from public fountains' — delivered with genuine wistfulness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. 'Bloated raccoon carcass' as the specific task Leslie would miss is perfectly absurd and perfectly Leslie — she's nostalgic for genuinely disgusting work because she loves the literal hands-on nature of her job. The question format ('Have I really pulled my last...?') adds a beautiful tragic dimension. Only Leslie Knope could say this line with complete sincerity. Exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, no, I would not have started the sentence if I knew Larry was the only one here.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'The public forum will be run by...' and scans the room for volunteers.
jokes.punchline: Larry is the only person present, forcing her to give him the responsibility — her horror at the realization interrupts her own sentence.
jokes.explanation: Great structural joke — Leslie backed herself into a corner with her own rhetorical sentence and is now trapped. 'I would not have started the sentence if I knew Larry was the only one here' is self-aware and funny. The joke also works as a commentary on the Larry-abuse running gag from a fresh angle.

jokes.text: I-I somehow ran my belt through a slat in this chair so I'm kind of... I'm kind of stuck to it now.
jokes.setup: Larry has been asked to come in and handle the public forum — a vote of confidence for him.
jokes.punchline: His triumphant entrance is immediately undercut by being physically stuck to a chair via belt — and he can't explain how he got there.
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry gag — the universe conspires against him even in his moment of near-triumph. Getting his belt stuck in a chair is specific and believably Larryesque. 'I-I somehow' suggests even he doesn't understand how it happened.

jokes.text: Great. [deadpan reaction shot after Larry announces he's stuck to a chair]
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been forced to entrust the public forum to Larry, who immediately announces he's stuck to a chair.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's single-word 'Great' — delivered as a flat defeat rather than genuine enthusiasm — is the button on the joke.
jokes.explanation: One-word reaction jokes live or die on delivery and context. Here, 'Great' is perfect because it requires the audience to do the work — Leslie's flat affect does all the comedy. Minimal but effective.

jokes.text: I once forgot to brush my teeth for five weeks.
jokes.setup: Andy is sharing his secrets with Ron to 'even it out.'
jokes.punchline: First secret: he once went five weeks without brushing his teeth — stated as if this is an embarrassing anomaly rather than a plausible regular occurrence for Andy.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy secret — the joke is partly that we believe him completely and partly that five weeks seems both specific and plausible.

jokes.text: I don't know who Al Gore is. And at this point I'm too afraid to ask.
jokes.setup: Andy continues sharing secrets with Ron.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know who Al Gore is — and more specifically, has reached the point of being 'too afraid to ask' because too much time has passed.
jokes.explanation: The 'too afraid to ask' extension is what elevates this from 'Andy is ignorant' to something more — the universal feeling of being embarrassed to ask something you feel you should know, applied to Al Gore. Very quotable.

jokes.text: When they say 2% milk, I don't know what the other 98% is.
jokes.setup: Andy's secrets continue.
jokes.punchline: He's genuinely puzzled by 2% milk — 2% of what? The secret is his dairy ignorance.
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist confession — Andy's 2% milk confusion is both relatable (it IS slightly confusing) and characteristically taken to an extreme. The phrasing 'the other 98%' is perfect.

jokes.text: When I was a baby, my head was so big scientists did experiments on me.
jokes.setup: Andy's secrets list continues.
jokes.punchline: His baby head was so large it attracted scientific attention — a secret that implies both unusual physiology and unexplained government involvement.
jokes.explanation: A lovely piece of Andy lore — the specificity of 'scientists' (not doctors) did experiments adds the right absurdist flavor. It also somehow explains a lot about Andy.

jokes.text: I once threw beer at a swan, and then it attacked my niece Rebecca.
jokes.setup: Andy's secrets continue, each more revealing than the last.
jokes.punchline: He threw beer at a swan — possibly understandable — but then the swan attacked his niece Rebecca, which is both dark and specific (we now know Rebecca exists and has been traumatized).
jokes.explanation: The best of Andy's secrets. 'And then it attacked my niece Rebecca' is the perfect punchline — the specificity of Rebecca's name makes it feel real, the consequence (swan attack on a child) is dark, and Andy is confessing this as a shameful secret rather than taking responsibility. The economy is excellent; maximum incident in minimum words. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: That'll do, Andrew.
jokes.setup: Andy has delivered a monologue of absurd secrets.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response — 'That'll do, Andrew' — delivered with Ron's characteristic flat gravity, both stopping the list and implying he's heard enough (which is a lot for Ron).
jokes.explanation: 'That'll do, Andrew' is an extremely Ron phrase — the Babe reference ('That'll do, pig') elevated by the use of Andy's formal name 'Andrew.' Ron calling him Andrew suggests both affection and that this has gotten somewhat serious. Perfect economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Watch cologne. Cologne for watches.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to cheer Tom up and has brought a gift.
jokes.punchline: The gift is 'watch cologne' — cologne specifically for watches. Ben explains it in case Tom doesn't understand, which makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A perfect absurdist Tom-world joke — 'watch cologne' is exactly the kind of pointless luxury that Tom's world would produce and Ben would give him. Ben's clarification ('Cologne for watches') is the perfect beat — he's not sure Tom knows what it is but has bought it anyway. Original concept, extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Things used to make me so happy. But I've grown a lot in the last year. Now I just want one big thing, my own restaurant, named after me, that makes me so much money I can buy anything I want.
jokes.setup: Tom is reflecting on his personal growth after the restaurant dream hits an obstacle.
jokes.punchline: His 'growth' is revealed as extremely superficial — he's gone from being excited by small material things to wanting one giant, greedy thing. The pivot 'I've grown a lot' → 'now I just want obscene wealth' is a perfect Tom joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom character joke — the structure builds sincere personal growth rhetoric and pivots to 'so much money I can buy anything I want.' The word 'named after me' in the middle of the list is also funny — Tom's ego is baked into his dream at every level. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I didn't want Tom to leave, so I said all these bad things about the restaurant, so he wouldn't like them. / Damn, we should have coordinated. I don't want to lose that weird little elf either. That's why I showed him all those crappy places. / Oh, I thought you were just bad at your job.
jokes.setup: April reveals she sabotaged the restaurant search to keep Tom from leaving.
jokes.punchline: Ben reveals he did the same thing — then April's response 'Oh, I thought you were just bad at your job' lands as both an insult to Ben and a reveal that April's sabotage was more deliberate than Ben's.
jokes.explanation: Three-part joke with a great structure: (1) April's confession, (2) Ben's mirror confession, (3) April's 'Oh, I thought you were just bad at your job' — which simultaneously compliments her own planning and insults Ben. 'Weird little elf' as a term of endearment for Tom is also a lovely character detail.

jokes.text: I think the slogan should be 'Pawnee, home of crackers, the orangest goldfish in Indiana.'
jokes.setup: Larry opens the public forum for slogan suggestions.
jokes.punchline: First suggestion: a slogan promoting a specific goldfish named Crackers as the orangest goldfish in Indiana — a hyper-local, bizarrely specific civic pride point.
jokes.explanation: The absurd specificity of 'home of Crackers, the orangest goldfish in Indiana' is classic Pawnee civic absurdism — the kind of thing a real small town resident would genuinely propose with complete seriousness.

jokes.text: Who even needs a slogan? / Well, now, that is an interesting point. / No, that's my slogan idea. 'Who even needs a slogan?' And then a big picture of me flipping everybody off.
jokes.setup: Someone at the forum rhetorically asks 'Who even needs a slogan?' — Larry takes it as a point of discussion.
jokes.punchline: The person clarifies it IS their slogan suggestion — including 'a big picture of me flipping everybody off' as the visual component.
jokes.explanation: Excellent three-beat joke: the rhetorical question, Larry's sincere engagement with it, and the reveal that it WAS a slogan pitch — with the addition of 'a big picture of me flipping everybody off' as the visual element. The photo-of-flipping-off detail is inspired.

jokes.text: Butt stick! Butt stick! Butt stick! [crowd chants]
jokes.setup: The Douche nation members push for 'Home of the stick up Leslie Knope's butt' at the public forum.
jokes.punchline: The crowd begins chanting 'Butt stick! Butt stick!' — a civic meeting has devolved into a rallying chant for an absurd slogan.
jokes.explanation: The chanting works as cringe comedy and escalation of the democratic chaos Leslie has unleashed. 'Butt stick' as a crowd chant is funny by sheer repetition and context.

jokes.text: I've lived in Pawnee my whole life and it could be a strange place, but overall it's a warm, and wonderful town. My idea for a slogan is, 'When you're here, then you're home.'
jokes.setup: After the chaos of Butt Stick chanting, a sincere resident offers a genuinely heartfelt slogan.
jokes.punchline: The slogan itself is lovely — and then it turns out to be misspelled, undercutting the entire earnest moment.
jokes.explanation: The setup is the sincerity — after chaos, a sweet moment — which makes the grammar error deflation funnier. The joke works because the woman is clearly proud of her printed-up slogan.

jokes.text: The sweet older woman's slogan 'When you're here, then you're home' — with 'then' spelled wrong, escalating to multiple people arguing about whether 'you're' is also spelled wrong
jokes.setup: A heartfelt older woman offers a genuinely lovely slogan suggestion and has had it printed up professionally
jokes.punchline: The slogan has a grammar error ('then' vs 'than'), which Larry catches, which leads to a second person saying 'you're' is also wrong (it isn't), which devolves into a full grammar argument while the kind woman's heartfelt idea is lost in procedural chaos
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed cringe sequence. The comedy escalates: typo (relatable) → Larry catches it (surprisingly competent) → someone confidently corrects a non-error ('you're' is right) → Leslie trying not to intervene while whispering to Ben. The subplot of Leslie desperately wanting to correct everyone while trying to delegate is the real heart of the joke. Good character integration for Leslie's dilemma.

jokes.text: Hm... there's... that's... that's spelled wrong. / Stay strong. Let them work it out. / Back off. / 'You're' is spelled wrong. It should be 'y-o-u-r.' / Oops, I didn't catch it. Thank you. / No, no, no, she made a possessive. She's getting further away.
jokes.setup: The kind woman's slogan has spelling errors. Larry begins to address them. Leslie is watching from afar trying not to intervene.
jokes.punchline: A grammar debate erupts among forum attendees, with multiple people giving conflicting corrections while Leslie desperately coaches Larry through an earpiece and the slogan submitter's confidence erodes.
jokes.explanation: Extended cringe sequence with great escalation — Leslie forced to watch from afar while a grammar debate derails the sincere slogan. 'She's getting further away' as a crisis update is particularly good. The joke works on multiple levels: Leslie's inability to let go, the Pawnee public's grammar chaos, and Larry's well-intentioned incompetence.

jokes.text: Man, the places that came on the market today are way nicer than the listings we saw yesterday. I know, crazy, right? Real estate.
jokes.setup: Tom is suddenly finding great restaurant spaces after April and Ben conspired to sabotage the previous viewings.
jokes.punchline: April covers with 'crazy, right? Real estate.' — the most non-specific possible explanation, delivered as if Tom should just accept market volatility as the explanation.
jokes.explanation: April's cover story — 'I know, crazy, right? Real estate.' — is perfectly April. She doesn't elaborate, doesn't offer details, just says 'real estate' as if that explains everything. Tom apparently accepts this.

jokes.text: The grammatically-corrected slogan is approved — Leslie held herself back the whole time
jokes.setup: Leslie has been desperately restraining herself from correcting the process
jokes.punchline: The vote passes and something gets approved — Leslie has succeeded by doing nothing, which is almost physically painful for her
jokes.explanation: Payoff to the delegation arc. The comedy is in Leslie's internal struggle — she didn't intervene, the world didn't end. More of a character beat than a joke per se, but has genuine comedic weight.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Are you listening to yourself?' — after Leslie says 'Trust Larry'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ben to 'Trust Larry' as a delegation mantra
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'Are you listening to yourself?' treats 'Trust Larry' as an objectively irrational statement that requires reality-checking
jokes.explanation: A solid reaction beat. Ben as Leslie's reality anchor works well here. The joke is primarily in 'Trust Larry' (#79) — this is the button. Good economy.

jokes.text: Tom's future restaurant space has nice properties but the realtor 'doesn't know' about the two helipads on his wish list — 'Does it have one helipad?'
jokes.setup: The realtor finds a great property within Tom's budget
jokes.punchline: Tom's list included two helipads; the realtor doesn't know about one helipad either, but Tom accepts this as a reasonable opening negotiating position
jokes.explanation: Tom's 'must-have' list including two helipads for a restaurant budget deal is perfectly Tom — aspirational to the point of delusion. 'Does it have one helipad?' as a compromise position is a great beat.

jokes.text: Does it have one helipad? / I don't know.
jokes.setup: Tom's wish list included 'two helipads.' The realtor says the new space has everything except the two helipads.
jokes.punchline: Tom's follow-up is whether it has ONE helipad — and the realtor genuinely doesn't know, suggesting one helipad is ambiguously plausible.
jokes.explanation: Tom's downward negotiation from two helipads to one is a great character beat — he's scaling back his dreams just barely. The realtor's 'I don't know' implies one helipad is within the realm of possibility, which is also funny.

jokes.text: You fixed the mistakes. / I held it together for the entire meeting. Let me have this one. / I'm done micromanaging. I promise. / Then I'm sure you are okay with the fact that they installed the sign the wrong way and it's welcoming you to Pawnee as you're leaving. / What? No! Oh, son of a...
jokes.setup: Leslie has triumphantly restrained herself from micromanaging the forum. She presents the slogan result with pride.
jokes.punchline: The sign was installed backwards — it welcomes people to Pawnee as they're leaving. Leslie immediately breaks her promise not to micromanage.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural payoff — Leslie's growth moment is immediately undermined by a new problem. 'Son of a...' is the right button: she's broken exactly the promise she just made. The sign-backwards detail is also a perfect real-world gag.

jokes.text: Leslie, I love you, very much. But this is the stupidest thing you've ever said. You'd be amazing. And everyone's gonna be in awe of how amazing you are, so just shut your mouth.
jokes.setup: Leslie confesses she's afraid she might fail at the national parks job — that she might not be good at it.
jokes.punchline: Ben's response begins with sincere 'I love you, very much' and immediately pivots to 'this is the stupidest thing you've ever said' — then delivers a passionate endorsement while telling her to 'shut your mouth.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's emotionally strongest jokes — the structure is (1) sincere declaration of love, (2) brutal dismissal ('stupidest thing you've ever said'), (3) passionate advocacy, (4) 'shut your mouth.' The comedy comes from the complete sincerity of all four beats simultaneously. Ben's bluntness-as-love is perfectly him, and the joke earns its laughs because it's also genuinely sweet.

jokes.text: Hey, are we leaving or entering? We've been driving around in circles. You're...
jokes.setup: Leslie just dealt with the backwards sign. Tom drives up with April.
jokes.punchline: Tom is confused by the sign — they've been circling because they can't tell if they're entering or leaving Pawnee — which is a direct visual consequence of the backwards sign.
jokes.explanation: A nice tag to close the episode — the backwards sign joke gets one more beat with Tom and April literally lost because of it. 'We've been driving around in circles' earns its callback status. The cut-off 'You're...' is a good button, letting the audience infer Leslie's meltdown.

tmdb_overview: Leslie throws a hasty Galentine's Day in an attempt to find a replacement for Ann. Tom and Ben look to finalize a deal on tents for the Unity Concert, while Ron finds himself looking after Andy.
insight: Mid-tier character work carries a thin-plot episode through 59 jokes at 2.18-per-minute pace.
